lessons.title: Climate risks for South African farms
lessons.html:
Climate risks for South African farms

South African farming has always dealt with variable rainfall, but climate change is increasing temperatures and the frequency of extreme events. Recent droughts, such as the severe drought affecting the Western Cape around 2015 to 2018 and widespread summer-rainfall droughts linked to El Nino, and floods in KwaZulu-Natal and the Eastern Cape, show the scale of the risk.

Main climate risks

RiskEffects on cropsEffects on livestock
DroughtCrop failure, lower yields, irrigation limitsVeld loss, forced sales, low conception
Heat wavesPollination failure, heat stress at floweringHeat stress, lower milk yield and fertility, deaths in intensive units
Heavy rain and floodsErosion, waterlogging, lost inputsDrowning, disease outbreaks, damaged infrastructure
Hail and frostDirect crop damageExposure losses in young stock
Shifting seasonsUnreliable planting windowsChanging pest and disease ranges, for example ticks
Veld firesLoss of grazing and cropsAnimal deaths, fence and infrastructure loss

Assessing farm vulnerability

  1. Review long-term rainfall and temperature records for the farm or nearest station.
  2. Identify which enterprises and resources are most exposed: dryland lands, water sources, high-value intensive units.
  3. List current coping measures: fodder reserves, insurance, water storage, drought-tolerant cultivars.
  4. Identify gaps and prioritise actions by risk and cost.

Use seasonal forecasts from the South African Weather Service and agricultural advisory services to inform planting and stocking decisions, while remembering they give probabilities, not certainties.

Climate risk also affects the value chain: drought raises feed prices for livestock, floods damage roads to markets, and heat waves reduce worker productivity. Resilience planning should consider inputs, markets and people, not only the land.

lessons.title: Adaptation practices for crops and livestock
lessons.html:
Adaptation practices for crops and livestock

Crops

  • Conservation agriculture: minimum tillage, permanent soil cover and rotation increase infiltration, soil organic matter and water-holding capacity.
  • Drought-tolerant and early-maturing cultivars, and crops such as sorghum and cowpeas in marginal areas.
  • Flexible planting: plant only once adequate soil moisture is present; adjust populations to expected rainfall.
  • Efficient irrigation: drip or well-maintained centre pivots, scheduling by soil moisture.
  • Diversification: several crops with different timing reduce the chance of total failure.
  • Insurance: crop insurance against hail, drought or multi-peril where available.

Livestock

  • Conservative stocking: stock below the long-term grazing capacity so there is reserve for dry years.
  • Drought plan: set trigger dates (for example, if a set amount of rain has not fallen by a certain month) to reduce numbers early by selling culls and weaners, before prices fall and condition is lost.
  • Fodder banks: hay, silage and drought-tolerant fodder crops such as spineless cactus or saltbush in arid areas.
  • Adapted breeds: indigenous breeds such as Nguni cattle and Dorper sheep tolerate heat, ticks and poor veld better than many exotic breeds.
  • Heat stress management: shade, extra water points, cooling in dairies and intensive units, working animals in the cool of the day.
  • Water security: maintain boreholes and reservoirs, protect springs, and add storage.

Climate-smart resource management

  • Protect wetlands and riparian zones, which buffer floods and droughts.
  • Clear invasive alien plants that use large amounts of water, as required under CARA (Act 43 of 1983).
  • Build firebreaks and maintain fire-fighting equipment; join the local fire protection association.
  • Use renewable energy, such as solar pumping, to reduce costs and dependence on grid supply.

Planning and finance

Build a cash reserve or access to credit for bad years, and plan the timing of capital spending. Keep good records to support insurance claims and any drought relief applications.

Key points

  • Drought, heat, floods, hail, fire and shifting seasons are key climate risks.
  • Assess vulnerability and use seasonal forecasts as probabilities.
  • Conservation agriculture and adapted cultivars build crop resilience.
  • Conservative stocking, drought triggers and fodder banks protect livestock.
  • Protect water, wetlands and veld; plan finance for bad years.
